newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade protesters woo police with charm campaign.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade protesters woo police with charm campaign.

text.p: Serbian pro-democracy demonstrators marking Orthodox Christmas Day with their 51st consecutive day of protest wooed police on Tuesday with a charm offensive to win them over to their cause.
As protesters headed towards Republic Square, private cars hooted an ironic welcome at a long convoy of police vehicles heading for the main Terazije throughfare.

The Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition called for friendly conversations between citizens and security forces and said it would distribute letters to police explaining the reasons for the protests.
"Get on with this thing so we can all go home," one policeman urged protesters gathered in Republic Square.
Another blamed President Slobodan Milosevic for making both demonstrators and police turn out in freezing temperatures.

"The majority of members of the Serbian Interior Ministry disagree with the decision of the Socialist Party of Serbia that police should occupy the centre of Belgrade and other Serbian towns," Zajedno said in a statement.
Reporters said 50 people surrounded one traffic policeman as part of the "Talk to Cops" campaign. The police presence was bigger than usual but police stayed in their vehicles.
On Monday, student leaders met Yugoslav army commander General Momcilo Perisic, who expressed sympathy for their cause.
"This anniversary march, on Christmas Day, must be another mass gathering. Let us assemble in Republic Square to wish one another Merry Christmas," said Vuk Draskovic, an opposition leader.

Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators flouting a ban on street protests paralysed central Belgrade on Monday in an Orthodox Christmas Eve procession to St Sava Cathedral for midnight mass, their biggest rally yet.
On Monday night, the Yugoslav Left (JUL) party led by Milosevic's wife Mirjana Markovic said a bomb had been thrown at its headquarters, causing damage but no injuries.
Zajedno leaders denied involvement in the bombing. Draskovic said it had been staged to provoke a state of emergency.
Romanian President Emil Constantinescu added his voice to the international chorus urging the Yugoslav authorities to validate the disputed municipal election results.

"The president of Romania believes that prolonging the crisis in Yugoslavia will affect the democratic process there, the country's return to the international community and have a negative effect on regional stability," he said.

More worrying for Milosevic, the speaker of the Montenegrin parliament, Svetozar Marovic, said the events in Serbia were causing extensive damage to Yugoslavia, which is made up of Serbia and Montenegro.
No one has the right to do this, not even the president of Serbia and "especially not his wife with her phantom organization which apparently has brought many problems to Serbia," he said.
Unless a democratic solution was found urgently "Montenegro would have to think seriously about its next moves," he said.
Tiny Montenegro has pursued a vigorous privatisation programme. Some businessmen believe Montenegro would fare better alone without sharing Serbia's international embarrassment.
An inquiry by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) has verified opposition claims to have won voting in 15 of Serbia's 18 largest cities, including Belgrade.
In Nis, one of the 15 disputed municipalities, students posted hundreds of death notices announcing a "commemoration for the Municipal Assembly" scheduled for Wednesday.

Serbia's Socialist government grudgingly admitted last week that Zajedno prevailed in a few of the smaller cities but insisted that in other districts no party gained a majority or the results were inconclusive and needed further study.
